steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key ways in which RNA (ribonucleic acid) differs from DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)

1. Sugar component  
   • RNA: Ribose (has a hydroxyl group –OH on the 2′ carbon)  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks the 2′-OH; has –H instead)  
   → The extra –OH makes RNA more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • RNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Uracil (U)  
   • DNA: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, Thymine (T)  
   → Uracil in RNA replaces thymine in DNA.

3. Strandedness and overall shape  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded; can fold back on itself to form complex 3-D structures (hairpins, loops).  
   • DNA: Typically double-stranded, forming a long, antiparallel double helix (B-form is most common).

4. Length and size  
   • RNA molecules are generally much shorter (a few dozen to several thousand nucleotides) than chromosomes made of DNA (millions to billions of base pairs).

5. Stability  
   • DNA is highly stable (good for long-term genetic storage).  
   • RNA is relatively unstable and more prone to enzymatic degradation (appropriate for transient messages).

6. Function  
   • DNA: Long-term storage of hereditary information; blueprint of the cell.  
   • RNA: Diverse, mostly short-term roles:  
     – mRNA (messenger) carries genetic code from DNA to ribosome.  
     – rRNA (ribosomal) forms the core of ribosomes and catalyzes peptide-bond formation.  
     – tRNA (transfer) brings amino acids for protein synthesis.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.) control gene expression.  
     – Some RNA molecules act as enzymes (ribozymes) or as genetic material in certain viruses.

7. Cellular location  
   • DNA: Confined mainly to the nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts in eukaryotes).  
   • RNA: Synthesized in the nucleus but functions largely in the cytoplasm; some varieties stay in the nucleus or other organelles.

8. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA replicates (is copied) during S-phase of the cell cycle via DNA polymerases.  
   • RNA is transcribed from DNA templates by RNA polymerases; it is not self-replicating in cells (some RNA viruses are exceptions).

9. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA has elaborate repair systems to maintain fidelity.  
   • RNA generally lacks such repair; errors usually just lower the lifetime or effectiveness of the particular RNA molecule.

10. Evolutionary perspective  
   • Many scientists propose an “RNA world” in early evolution, where RNA performed both informational and catalytic roles before DNA and proteins dominated. 

Summary: DNA is a stable, double-stranded, thymine-containing polymer that stores long-term genetic information. RNA is a more reactive, usually single-stranded, uracil-containing polymer that serves multiple short-term and regulatory functions—including acting as the intermediary for protein synthesis and, in some cases, as a catalytic molecule or even a viral genome.
